prompts.L3:
Please expand the following bullet points into a complete, well-structured text:

- The train announces its approach through the singing, trembling tracks and a distant hum before it becomes visible.
- The speakers instinctively crouch, play on the sleepers and rails, and listen closely for the oncoming train.
- The train connects the resource-rich interior to the capital, carrying felled timber and bauxite.
- The speakers fear the train’s immense power, which can flatten metal, destroy traffic, and issue a threatening whistle and steam.
- The seemingly endless twin rails symbolize forward movement and hope while echoing the force and clatter of the train and the forest resources it transports.

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Long, The, Train

outputs.L1:
Long before you see the train,  
The tracks sing and tremble.  
Long before you know the direction  
The train comes from, a hum  
Announces that it will soon arrive.  

So we tend to drop on all fours  
Even before we look left or right.  
We skip the sleepers or walk  
Along, balancing on a rail.  

We talk about the capital,  
Where the train ends its run,  
Coming from the interior, stacked with  
The outsized trunks of felled  
Trees and open-topped cars of bauxite.  

We always hide from it, unsure  
What the train will do if we  
Stand next to the tracks.  
It flattens our nails into knives.  
It obliterates any traffic  
Caught by it at crossroads.  
It whistles a battle cry,  
Steam from the engine—a mood  
Not to be trifled with, or else.  

Rails without beginning or end,  
Twinned hopes always at your back,  
Always up front, signaling you on:  
Double oxen, hoof-stomp, temper  
Tantrum, stampede, clatter,  
Matter, head-splitter—hear us,  
Stooped with an ear to the line:  
Greenheart, mora, baromalli, purpleheart,  
Crabwood, kabakalli, womara.
outputs.L2:
Before the locomotive comes into view,  
the rails quiver and begin their song.  
Before we can tell which way it approaches,  
a low vibration warns us  
that it will soon appear.

Without first checking either side,  
we often crouch close to the ground.  
We leap from tie to tie  
or steady ourselves along one steel rail.

We speak of the capital,  
the final stop for a train arriving from inland,  
loaded with enormous trunks from cut trees  
and uncovered wagons filled with bauxite.

Uncertain what might happen  
if we remain beside the line,  
we always conceal ourselves.  
The train presses our nails into blades,  
destroys any vehicle trapped at a crossing,  
and releases a whistle like a war shout.  
Steam surging from its engine  
warns against challenging its temper.

The paired tracks seem endless,  
with no visible source or destination—  
two promises stretching behind you  
and beckoning from ahead.

Like yoked oxen, pounding hooves,  
a fit of rage, a charging herd:  
rattle and force, skull-splitting noise.  
Listen to us, bent low,  
one ear placed against the rail—

greenheart, mora, baromalli,  
purpleheart, crabwood, kabakalli, womara.
outputs.L3:
Before the train comes into view, its approach is announced by the railway itself: the tracks seem to sing and tremble, while a distant hum gradually grows louder. Drawn by these sounds, the speakers instinctively crouch beside the railway, playing on the sleepers and rails while listening closely for the approaching engine.

The train is more than an impressive machine; it also provides an important connection between the resource-rich interior and the capital. Its wagons carry felled timber and bauxite, transporting the wealth of the forest and the land toward the city. Yet the speakers are deeply aware of its immense and potentially destructive power. They fear a force capable of flattening metal and crushing anything caught in its path. Its piercing whistle, bursts of steam, and thunderous movement make it appear both threatening and overwhelming.

At the same time, the twin rails stretching into the distance suggest progress, movement, and hope. Their seemingly endless lines point forward, linking remote regions to the wider world. However, they also echo the relentless clatter and force of the train, as well as the exploitation and transportation of the forest’s natural resources. The railway therefore represents both possibility and danger: it promises connection and advancement while carrying a power that inspires fear and transforms the landscape.
outputs.L4:
The poem presents a group of children crouched beside railway tracks, listening and waiting for the approach of a freight train. From their low, vulnerable position, the train seems enormous and almost supernatural. Before it is fully visible, it announces itself through vibration and sound: the rails tremble, the ground shudders, and the mechanical rhythm grows steadily louder. These sensory details allow the reader to experience the train as the children do—not simply as a machine, but as a powerful presence that can be heard and felt long before it arrives.

The children’s response combines terror with fascination. They know that the train is dangerous, and their closeness to the tracks intensifies the sense of risk. Yet they cannot look away. The noise, speed, smoke, and weight of the passing carriages create an overwhelming spectacle. The poem’s rhythm likely echoes the pounding of wheels against rails, while repeated sounds reproduce the train’s relentless movement. In this way, language becomes part of the action: the poem does not merely describe the train but imitates its approach and passage.

The train’s cargo gives this dramatic encounter a broader economic and political meaning. Laden with timber and bauxite from the interior, it carries the natural wealth of the land toward the capital. Its movement links remote forests and mining regions to the urban center, turning raw materials into commodities and the landscape into a source of profit. The train therefore represents industrial development and modern transportation, but it also suggests extraction. What is taken from the interior passes rapidly before the children, heading elsewhere, while they remain beside the tracks as observers.

This contrast complicates the idea of progress. The railway appears to connect different parts of the country, yet it may also expose the unequal distribution of the benefits produced by that connection. The children witness valuable resources being transported away, but the poem does not necessarily show them sharing in the prosperity those resources promise. The train embodies modernity, power, and economic movement, while the children’s crouched position emphasizes their smallness and limited control. They are physically close to the machinery of development but socially distant from the forces directing it.

At the same time, the train is more than a threatening instrument of industry. Because it travels between the interior and the capital, it also carries the idea of distant places and possible futures. To the children, the tracks seem almost endless, stretching beyond the familiar world. Their fascination may therefore contain a measure of longing. The train suggests escape, travel, opportunity, and contact with a larger world, even as its speed and violence make those possibilities appear inaccessible or dangerous.

The poem ultimately holds these meanings in tension. The train is frightening and mesmerizing, destructive and promising, familiar and mysterious. Through the children’s perspective, the railway becomes a place where private emotion meets national history. Their fear reflects the immediate danger of the passing machine, while their wonder points toward dreams of movement and change. Along the endless tracks, extraction, modernity, inequality, fear, and hope converge, making the train both a material force and a complex symbol of the future.
outputs.L5:
## The Long Train

The long train moved steadily through the quiet countryside, its windows glowing against the evening sky. Inside, passengers read, whispered, and watched distant towns pass by. No one knew exactly what waited at the final station, but the rhythm of the wheels made the journey feel timeless. For a little while, the train carried them beyond ordinary life, toward a place filled with possibility.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a free-verse poem from a child’s perspective about hearing a freight train approach in Guyana, mentioning timber, bauxite, railway games, danger, and native hardwood trees.
counterfactuals.output:
Before I see it,  
the rails begin whispering  
under my bare feet.

Far down the line  
a freight train coughs awake,  
dragging timber from the forest,  
bauxite red as sunset  
packed in iron cars.

We children stop our railway games—  
coins on the track,  
ears to the steel,  
daring each other  
to wait one second more.

But danger has a heavy voice.

It grows louder  
through greenheart, mora, wallaba—  
native hardwood trees  
standing dark and watchful  
beside the clearing.

The engine bursts around the bend,  
horn splitting the hot Guyana air.

We scatter, laughing and afraid,  
while the long train shakes the earth  
and carries the deep country  
away.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a vivid poem in Caribbean-inflected English about children living beside train tracks that carry logs and minerals from the interior to the capital.
counterfactuals.output:
**Trackside Pickney**

Morning crack open like ripe pawpaw,  
gold light spilling on zinc-roof yard,  
and the pickney dem wake to iron thunder—  
train coming, train coming,  
long as a hard-luck story.

From deep bush it drag the greenheart logs,  
bauxite red as old blood,  
stone and ore from the belly of country,  
all bound for the capital  
where glass towers catch the sun  
and never send it back.

Beside the line, barefoot children  
count each wagon—  
one, two, twenty, plenty—  
their voices bright above the clatter.  
Dust dress their ankles.  
Smoke plait their hair.  
A little boy lift one hand  
and the driver answer with a horn  
big enough to shake mango from tree.

The girls race the last carriage,  
skirts flying like kiskadee wings;  
they know every bend, every loose fishplate,  
every place the sleepers sink in rain.  
They know when mahogany passing,  
when manganese passing,  
when the whole dark wealth of the interior  
roll through without stopping.

Still, evening sweeten the galvanize yard.  
Granny turn cassava on the fire.  
Somebody beat a bucket like drum.  
The children chalk small houses  
on the stones between tracks—  
houses with gardens, schools,  
windows wide to sea-breeze.

And when night train bawl  
toward the city’s electric glow,  
the pickney dem lie close, listening  
to the rails sing under their dreams:

One day, not everything passing.  
One day, something staying—  
book and bread, clean water,  
a future strong as greenheart,  
a morning bright as mineral  
before the earth get break.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a nostalgic, sensory poem titled “Listening for the Train,” ending with a rhythmic list of Guyanese woods such as greenheart, mora, baromalli, purpleheart, crabwood, kabakalli, and womara.
counterfactuals.output:
# Listening for the Train

At dusk, we set our ears against the rails,  
though rust had reddened every silver mile,  
and waited where the cane fields breathed molasses,  
where frogs stitched rain into the trenches  
and kerosene lamps flowered in the houses.

Somewhere, a pot lid rang in a kitchen.  
Smoke from the fires curled through guava leaves.  
The Demerara darkened, broad and patient,  
carrying old voices under its skin.  
We tasted salt, burnt sugar, green mango,  
felt mosquitoes write their names on our ankles.

“Listen,” you whispered—  
and the night grew large around that word:  
a dog barking beyond the kokers,  
a bicycle bell, a market song fading,  
the long iron thunder we remembered  
more clearly than it ever came.

Years later, I still lean toward silence,  
waiting for the whistle to gather us home—  
past verandahs warm with laughter,  
past rain drumming zinc roofs,  
past sawdust bright as morning  
in the old timber yard,

where each name fell hard and musical,  
like wheels keeping time on vanished track:

**greenheart, mora—  
baromalli, purpleheart—  
crabwood, kabakalli—  
womara, womara.**
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an experimental poem that begins with the tracks singing before a train appears and uses sound, repetition, and violent imagery to convey the train’s power.
counterfactuals.output:
The tracks sing first—

thin silver throats  
          ting—ting—  
                    trembling under gravel,

a wire-song,
a warning worried raw:

coming coming  
       coming coming  
              come—

No train yet.

Only the rails humming their teeth,  
only the black ties counting:

one bone  
two bone  
three bone  
four—

Then—

              HORNNNNNN

the horizon splits its lip.

Iron shoulders through the wound,  
engine red-eyed,  
mouth full of thunder,  
wheels hacking sparks from stone.

Clang.  
     Clang.  
          CLANG—

It crushes distance flat,  
beats the earth with twelve steel fists,  
drags a chain of shrieking rooms  
through fields that buckle in its wake.

Go go go go—

The air is torn cloth.  
The night is nailed down.  
Every window flashes  
like a blade being drawn.

And after—

no train.

Only smoke uncoiling,  
only gravel stunned,

only the tracks still singing  
in their ruined, ringing mouths:

gone gone  
       gone gone  
              gone.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a free-verse monologue about children placing their ears against railway lines, balancing on rails, flattening nails into knives, and imagining the distant capital where the train completes its journey.
counterfactuals.output:
We were children, which meant  
the world had not yet learned  
to keep its secrets from us.

We laid our ears to the cold line,  
cheek against gravel,  
listening for the iron rumor—  
a tremor from beyond the hills,  
a message too deep for adults.

We walked the rails with arms outspread,  
each of us a wavering king  
above the weeds and splintered sleepers,  
falling, laughing, beginning again.

Sometimes we left nails on the track  
and waited at a distance  
for the train’s enormous hand  
to press them thin—  
little blades, bright and useless,  
treasures we carried home  
as if we had learned the craft of thunder.

But mostly we wondered where it went.

The capital, they said:  
a word taller than any building we knew,  
full of clocks, ministries, fountains,  
streets that continued after midnight,  
windows blazing floor upon floor.

We imagined the train arriving there  
with our fields still clinging to its wheels,  
our dust beneath its carriages,  
our faces briefly mirrored  
in every darkened pane.

And when the last wagon vanished,  
the rails kept shining between us,  
two narrow promises  
running straight toward a place  
we had never seen,

where surely the journey ended,  
where surely someone was waiting,  
ear pressed to the earth,  
listening for us.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
